column2: Why does diagnostic pathology begin before tissue reaches the laboratory?
column3: The clinical question determines what is sampled, how fast it is handled, and whether it must be sterile, unfixed, frozen or protected from light; an excellent test on the wrong specimen cannot answer the right question.

column2: How can a small biopsy mislead, and why must allocation of limited tissue be planned?
column3: It may miss a focal lesion or capture only necrosis, ulceration or reactive tissue; scarce tissue must be divided in advance among histology, microbiology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular tests.

column2: Why is block sampling at gross examination a deliberate trade-off?
column3: More blocks increase detection but consume time and tissue, while too few create false reassurance, so blocks target tumour, interface, normal tissue, deepest invasion and closest margins.

column3: Formalin cross-links proteins, but delayed, too short or excessive fixation alters staining and molecular assays, and decalcification may damage antigens and nucleic acids.

column2: Why is cellular atypia on a haematoxylin and eosin section not proof of malignancy?
column3: Repair, infection, radiation and degeneration can all produce alarming cells, so atypia is not synonymous with malignancy.

column3: No marker is perfectly specific, so a broad panel can yield contradictory incidental results; a staged panel tests plausible diagnoses in sequence while conserving tissue.

column3: Cytology is minimally invasive but gives less architecture than core biopsy or excision, and if uncertainty forces repeated procedures it may not be the least costly.

column3: A prognostic marker estimates outcome independent of a particular treatment, whereas a predictive marker estimates response or resistance to a specific therapy.
